Chance-corrected agreement between a judge and humans

Source: R/agreement.R
agreement.Rd

Reports how closely a set of judge labels agrees with human labels. Confidence intervals use a nonparametric item bootstrap. The categories the sample observed are held fixed across bootstrap draws so rare categories do not silently disappear from the estimand.

Usage

agreement(
  x,
  coefficients = NULL,
  conf_level = 0.95,
  n_boot = 2000,
  seed = NULL,
  label_levels = NULL,
  weights = c("unweighted", "linear", "quadratic", "ordinal"),
  rater_cols = NULL
)

Arguments

x

Either a yourhonor_calibration object or a data frame / tibble of ratings with one column per rater (see rater_cols). Rows with fewer than two observed ratings do not contribute, while partially observed multi-rater rows remain available to coefficients that support them.

For a calibration object every argument left at its default is inherited from the calibration (coefficients, conf_level, n_boot, seed, label_levels, and weights), so agreement(cal, n_boot = 50) reuses the stored seed and confidence level. When nothing is overridden the stored agreement table is returned unchanged.

coefficients

Character vector containing any of "cohen_kappa", "krippendorff_alpha", "gwet_ac1", and "gwet_ac2". NULL (the default) selects "cohen_kappa", "krippendorff_alpha", and "gwet_ac1", replacing "gwet_ac1" with its weighted counterpart "gwet_ac2" when weights is not "unweighted". Explicitly requesting "gwet_ac1" together with weights is an error rather than a silent substitution.

conf_level

Confidence level for the bootstrap interval.

n_boot

Positive number of bootstrap resamples. One set of item resamples is shared by every coefficient, so intervals from one call are computed on identical draws.

seed

Optional integer seed. The caller's random state is restored.

label_levels

Complete label universe in its intended order. Supplying this is strongly recommended for ordinal scales and rare classes. Labels are matched exactly: case and surrounding whitespace are significant, and empty or whitespace-only labels are rejected. Use NA for a missing or failed judgement.

weights

Agreement weights. "unweighted" treats labels as nominal; "linear", "quadratic", and "ordinal" use the order in label_levels and are Gwet's weight schemes as implemented by irrCAC (linear.weights(), quadratic.weights(), and ordinal.weights()). Every weighted coefficient, including "krippendorff_alpha", uses these schemes; weights = "ordinal" is Gwet's combinatorial ordinal weighting and is not Krippendorff's ordinal alpha, which weights by cumulative category frequencies.

rater_cols

Optional character vector naming the rater columns of a ratings data frame. When NULL, columns named human and judge are used if both exist; otherwise every column is treated as a rater. A message (class yourhonor_inferred_columns) reports the choice whenever inference ignored columns or fell back to all columns; supply rater_cols to choose explicitly. Cannot be combined with a calibration object, which carries its own ratings.

Value

A tibble with one row per coefficient and columns coefficient, estimate, conf_low, conf_high, se, n_items, conf_low_exact, n_input, n_raters, n_missing_rows, weights, n_boot_effective, boundary_degenerate, ci_reliable, status, and interpretation.

status is "ok" when the estimate and interval were computed, or one of "insufficient_items", "insufficient_variation", "insufficient_reference_variation", "invalid_rater_count", and "undefined". "insufficient_reference_variation" applies to a calibration object, whose human (consensus) reference must use at least two categories: against a single-class reference every chance-corrected coefficient is uninformative, and Gwet's AC1 in particular can read "almost perfect" while kappa reads zero. The rule applies to the full sample only: a bootstrap resample whose reference happens to hold one category still contributes its coefficient.

conf_low_exact is a resampling-free lower bound on the coefficient's own observed agreement pa, mapped onto its scale as (lower - pe) / (1 - pe) with the sample's chance term pe held fixed, then capped as described below. pa is the mean over items of each item's weighted pairwise agreement, so a near miss under weights earns its partial credit; Krippendorff's alpha's pa is (1 - eps) * A + eps, with A the mean weighted by each item's number of ratings r and eps = 1 / sum(r), and its bound is on A. Each item's agreement is bounded by the declared weights' range, 0 to 1, not by the weights between the categories the sample happened to show: a rare, distant disagreement the sample missed would otherwise make the bound overshoot. Declaring a level beyond the observed ones therefore lowers kappa's and alpha's bound even where it leaves their estimates unchanged. The bound is one-sided at level (1 + conf_level) / 2, like the lower end of the bootstrap interval. With two raters and no weights each item agrees or not, and the bound is Clopper-Pearson's. Otherwise each item's agreement lies between 0 and 1, and the bound is the binomial stop-loss bound for a mean of such values, which is never looser than Hoeffding's; for alpha with three or more rater columns it bounds alpha's ratio of rating-weighted agreement by inverting Hoeffding's relative-entropy test, so missing ratings widen it. On a perfect sample every route gives Clopper-Pearson's ((1 - conf_level) / 2)^(1 / n) for n items, except alpha with missing ratings, which is lower.

No sample's bound ranks above that of a perfect sample it can be corrected into: a correction gives every item whose ratings disagree one of its own ratings for all of them (in a calibration, the judge matching the human reference) and keeps the other items and the missing ratings, and the bound is capped at the worst such perfect sample's (for Gwet's coefficients, at or below it: their chance term is bounded from above rather than found exactly). Without the cap an error could rank above its own correction, because a rating moved into a rarer category, or into one the perfect sample never used, raises the chance disagreement 1 - pe that divides the bound's margin. The cap costs most at small n with rare categories, where a rare category seen only in disagreements lets a correction drop it: in simulation with 20 to 30 items and end categories of 1% to 3%, the share of samples whose AC2 bound reached 0.6 fell from 12% to 1% in the worst scenario (three raters, end categories of 3%, 30 items), while coverage was unchanged; from 100 items it moved the mean bound by about 0.004 at most. Two imperfect samples keep no such guarantee: correcting an error can lower the estimate itself (when it removes the only rating in a category from the chance term), so no bound that tracks the estimate can always rise with a correction.

As items accumulate the bound approaches the estimate, at a rate of about 1 / sqrt(n), for every coefficient, weighting and number of raters, provided 1 - pe stays away from 0, for the corrections too. For kappa and alpha that holds when the items the raters agree on use at least two categories in non-vanishing shares. Gwet's chance term for a correction always stays below 1, but on a wide quadratic scale the gap can be small (about 0.02 with six levels), so the cap can hold the bound down until a few thousand items.

It is exact (a finite-sample bound, not an asymptotic one) for observed agreement, not for the coefficient, because pe is itself estimated; in simulation (two and several raters, weighted and not, alpha with missing ratings, 30 to 1000 items) its coverage of the coefficient was at or above nominal, within simulation error. It does not depend on resampling, so it stays honest where the percentile bootstrap is optimistic: at small n, and on a perfect sample, whose bootstrap is a zero-width interval at 1. Because the bound on observed agreement is divided by 1 - pe, it is weak for kappa and alpha on imbalanced labels, whose pe is large: at 90/10 prevalence it stays far below the estimate until a few hundred items (a kappa of 0.92 on 100 items averaged about 0.63 in simulation), and it can fall below -1 (kappa's floor is -pe / (1 - pe)). Gwet's AC1 has a small pe there and is affected far less. It never exceeds estimate, is reported for every coefficient with status = "ok", and is NA otherwise. Policies assess the smaller of conf_low and conf_low_exact; see acceptance_policy().

ci_reliable is TRUE only when at least 30 resamples, and at least 80% of the requested resamples, produced a finite statistic, and the interval is not boundary_degenerate. With n_boot below 30 every interval is therefore unreliable. A perfect finite sample produces a zero-width nonparametric bootstrap, and that interval is flagged unreliable rather than treated as proof of population-perfect agreement; conf_low_exact is the usable lower bound there. The percentile bootstrap is also optimistic at small n (around 30 items or fewer), which is why policies also read conf_low_exact.

interpretation applies the Landis and Koch (1977) bands ("poor" below 0, then "slight", "fair", "moderate", "substantial", and "almost perfect" at 0.2 steps). Those bands were proposed for kappa; applied to alpha, AC1, or AC2 they are a heuristic reading aid, not a validated scale, and the same data can land in different bands under different coefficients.

Details

Chance agreement counts the categories some rater used, not every declared level: Gwet's AC1 and AC2 divide by the number of categories, so a declared level that no rater used would otherwise raise them on identical data (Cohen's kappa and Krippendorff's alpha are unaffected by unused levels). Unweighted, an unused declared level therefore changes no coefficient. Weighted coefficients still take their weights from the full declared scale, so an ordinal distance never depends on which levels were observed. An unused level still changes the weights between the observed levels, and every weighted chance term sums those weights: with linear weights and levels 1 to 3 observed, declaring a fourth level can move AC2's chance term from about 0.55 to 0.70 and so change AC2 itself. Kappa's and alpha's chance terms move too. For a level beyond the observed ones each weight scheme only rescales the distances between observed levels, so their observed agreement moves with the chance term and their estimates do not change (their conf_low_exact does; see below). A level between observed ones can change those distances and the weighted estimates with them.

Agreement is descriptive evidence, not a universal fitness gate. In particular, a high aggregate coefficient can coexist with zero recall on a rare, important class. Use report() with an explicit acceptance_policy() and inspect confusion_metrics() before making a deployment decision.

References

Gwet, K. L. (2014). Handbook of Inter-Rater Reliability (4th ed.). Advanced Analytics, LLC.

Landis, J. R., & Koch, G. G. (1977). The measurement of observer agreement for categorical data. Biometrics, 33(1), 159-174.

Examples

ratings <- data.frame(
  human = c("C", "C", "P", "I", "C", "P", "I", "C"),
  judge = c("C", "C", "C", "I", "C", "P", "P", "C")
)
agreement(ratings, n_boot = 200, seed = 1,
          label_levels = c("I", "P", "C"), weights = "ordinal",
          rater_cols = c("human", "judge"))
#> # A tibble: 3 × 16
#>   coefficient   estimate conf_low conf_high conf_low_exact    se n_items n_input

#> 1 cohen_kappa      0.758    0.352         1       -0.313   0.184       8       8
#> 2 krippendorff…    0.767    0.283         1       -0.341   0.194       8       8
#> 3 gwet_ac2         0.813    0.561         1       -0.00832 0.117       8       8
#> # ℹ 8 more variables: n_raters <int>, n_missing_rows <int>, weights <chr>,
